body.p: ARGUMENTS/ REMARKS
Status of Claims

Applicant submits this Amendment and Response to address the final Office Action dated January 31, 2024 ("Office Action"). Claims 5 and 18-20 were previously cancelled. Claims 9-17 were previously withdrawn. No claims have been added or cancelled herein. Claims 1 and 21 are amended, without adding any new matter and without intending to abandon or dedicate to the public any patentable subject matter. Therefore, claims 1-4, 6-8, and 21-23 are present for examination. Applicant respectfully requests reconsideration of this application as amended.

Claims 1 and 21 are rejected under 35 U.S.C. § 112(b) as being indefinite for failing to particularly point out and distinctly claim the subject matter regarded as the invention, due to the use of the term "precise" in the claims. Claims 2-4, 6-8, 22, and 23 are also rejected due to their dependency to claim 1 or 21.

Applicant respectfully disagrees with the Office Action's assertion, and submits that one of ordinary skill in the art would easily understand the term "precise" in light of the Specification. See, e.g., Application, Abstract, [0065]. However, in the interest of advancing prosecution, Applicant has amended claims 1 and 21 to remove the language in question, such that the present rejection is now moot.

For at least the foregoing reasons, Applicant respectfully submits that the rejections of the claims under 35 U.S.C. § 112 have been overcome, and respectfully requests that those rejections be withdrawn.

Claims 1-4, 6-8, and 21-23 are rejected under 35 U.S.C. § 101 for being directed to non- statutory subject matter. Applicant respectfully traverses this rejection and requests that it be withdrawn, for at least the following reasons.

The current test to determine whether a claim is directed toward patent eligible subject matter is the analysis based upon Alice Corp. Pty. Ltd. v. CLS Bank Int'l., 134 S. Ct. 2347 (2014) (hereinafter "Alice") and Mayo Collaborative Services v. Prometheus Laboratories, Inc., 132 S. Ct. 1289 (2011) (hereinafter "Mayo"). This test is essentially in two parts.

"Supreme Court precedent instructs us to 'first determine whether the claims at issue are directed to a patent-ineligible concept."' Enfish, LLC v. Microsoft Corp., No. 2015-2044, slip op. at *9 (Fed. Cir. May 12, 2016) (quoting Alice, at 2347) (hereinafter "Enfish").
As "[t]he Supreme Court has not established a definitive rule to determine what

constitutes as an 'abstract idea' sufficient to satisfy the first step of the Mayo/Alice inquiry," the Court has "found it sufficient to compare claims at issue to those claims already found to be directed to an abstract idea in previous cases." Id. (citing Alice). "If this threshold determination is met, we move to the second step of the inquiry and 'consider the elements of each claim both individually and "as an ordered combination" to determine whether the additional elements "transform the nature of the claim" into a patent-eligible application."' Id. (quoting Alice (quoting Mayo)).
The analysis of the claims at issue will be presented below, discussing the claims in Parts 1, 2A and 2B.
Step 1 - Determine whether the claim is directed to one of the statutory categories of invention.
Step 2A - If the claim is directed to one of the statutory categories of invention, determine if the claim is, as a whole, directed to a judicial exception.

Step 2B - If the claim is, as a whole, directed to a judicial exception, analyze the claim elements, both individually and as a whole, to determine if there are additional limitations that amount to significantly more than the abstract idea.

As explained below, the claims satisfy Part 1 as they are directed to at least one of the statutory categories of invention, as well as Part 2A, as the claims are not directed to a judicially recognized exception. While analysis under Part 2B should not be required, the claims also satisfy the significantly more than an abstract idea test for a number of reasons, including the fact that the claims are specifically limited to a specific technical field. For these reasons, as discussed below, the claims are directed to patent-eligible subject matter.
Step 1: The claims are directed to one of the statutory categories of invention.
Applicant agrees with the Examiner that all of the claims meet the requirements of step
Step 2A: Prong One - Evaluate Whether the Claim Recites a Judicial Exception
The Office Action asserts that the claims recite an abstract idea that falls into the
"Mental Processes" groupings. See Office Action ps. 3-4. Applicant respectfully disagrees.

Initially, Applicant submits that the claims are not directed toward mental processes. The October 2019 Update to the Revised Patent Subject Matter Eligibility ("October 2019 Update") states that "[c]laims do not recite a mental process when they do not contain limitations that can practically be performed in the human mind." See October 2019 Update p. 2 (Notice provided at 84 Fed. Reg. 55942 (Oct. 18, 2019); substance of the Update published at https://www.uspto.gov) (emphasis added). Claim 1 recites, inter alia, a robotic arm positionable in any pose and configured to support an object, registering a patient to a pre- operative image to enable the robotic arm to be positionable relative to the anatomical element, reregistering the patient to the pre-operative image based on the notification indicating that the relative pose of the first tracking device and the second tracking device has changed, and automatically positioning the robotic arm relative to the anatomical element after the relative pose has changed. Applicant respectfully submits that such actions cannot be practically performed in the human mind. For example, the registration process and the reregistration process enables a robotic arm to be positionable relative to an anatomical element and the robotic arm is automatically positioned relative to the anatomical element - actions that cannot be practically performed in the human mind. Accordingly, the claims are not directed toward mental processes.
Since the pending claims are not directed toward an abstract idea, the pending claims are patent eligible. Applicant respectfully requests reconsideration and withdrawal of the rejection.
Step 2A: Prong Two - Evaluate Whether the Claim, As a Whole, Integrates the Recited Judicial Exception into a Practical Application of the Exception
Although Applicant believes the claims are not directed toward a judicial exception,

and that further analysis under Step 2A, Prong Two is believed to be redundant, the claims are directed toward a practical application for at least the reason that they integrate the alleged judicial exception into a practical application.

The October 2019 Update indicates that "[in order to determine whether the claimed invention improves the functioning of a computer or other technology], first the specification should be evaluated to determine if the disclosure provides sufficient details such that one of ordinary skill in the art would recognize the claimed invention as providing an improvement. The specification need not explicitly set forth the improvement, but it must describe the invention such that the improvement would be apparent to one of ordinary skill in the art." Id. at 12. Then, "the claim must be evaluated to ensure that the claim itself reflect the disclosed improvement." Id. at 12.
The use of these technical solutions helps ensure proper registration and/or

reregistration during the surgical operation such that the robotic arm can be automatically positioned relative to the patient even after patient movement. Applicant submits that a person of ordinary skill in the art would, when viewing such a detailed disclosure, recognize the claimed invention as providing an improvement.

Moreover, such technical solutions are recited by the claims. Indeed, independent claim 1 recites a robotic arm positionable in any pose and configured to support an object, registering a patient to a pre-operative image to enable the robotic arm to be positionable relative to the

anatomical element, reregistering the patient to the pre-operative image based on the notification indicating that the relative pose of the first tracking device and the second tracking device has changed, and automatically positioning the robotic arm relative to the anatomical element after the relative pose has changed. Applicant submits that these claim features recite the disclosed improvement to ensure an accurate registration. Accordingly, the claim as a whole integrates the alleged judicial exception into a practical application.
Step 2B

Although Applicant submits that the currently pending claims are patent eligible under a Step 2A analysis as discussed above, Applicant also submits that the claims recite additional hardware elements that are sufficient to amount to "significantly more" than an abstract idea. For example, by affixing a first tracking device to a table and a second tracking device to an anatomical element having a pose relative to the table, patient movement relative to the table can be monitored. If patient movement is detected, then reregistration may occur and a robotic arm is automatically positioned relative to the patient before and after patient movement. Thus, the claims amount to "significantly more" than an abstract idea.

For at least the foregoing reasons, Applicant respectfully submits that the second prong of the eligibility test properly results in a determination of patent-eligibility, and respectfully requests that the rejection of claims 1-8 under 35 U.S.C. § 101 be withdrawn.

Claims 1, 2, 7, 8, and 21-23 are rejected under 35 U.S.C. § 103 as being obvious over International Patent Publication No. 2020/072335 to Nikou et al. ("Nikou") in view of U.S. Publication No. 2019/0321657 to Hale ("Hale"). Claim 3 is rejected under 35 U.S.C. § 103 as being obvious over Nikou in view of Hale, and further in view of U.S. Patent Publication No. 2014/0206990 to Epstein et al. ("Epstein"). Claim 6 is rejected under 35 U.S.C. § 103 as being obvious over Nikou in view of Hale in view of U.S. Patent Publication No. 2019/0090955 to Singh et al. ("Singh").

To establish aprimafacie case of obviousness, all claim limitations must first be taught or suggested by the prior art. See, e.g., DyStar Textilfarben GmbH & Co. Deutschland KG v. C.H. Patrick Co., 464 F.3d 1356, 1360 (Fed. Cir. 2006); 80 U.S.P.Q.2d 1641, 1645 (2006). "All

words in a claim must be considered in judging the patentability of that claim against the prior art." MPEP § 2143.03 (citing In re Wilson, 424 F.2d 1382, 1385, 165 USPQ 494, 496 (CCPA 1970)). The Examiner must then provide an explicit analysis of the motivation for combining the references. See KSR Int'l Co. v. Teleflex Inc., 550 U.S. 398, 418 (2007); 82 U.S.P.Q.2d 1385, 1396 (2007) ("a patent composed of several elements is not proved obvious merely by demonstrating that each of its elements was, independently, known in the prior art . . .."). While the Examiner can choose one of several exemplary rationales from the MPEP to support an obviousness rejection, all the rationales in the MPEP still require the Examiner to demonstrate that all the claim elements are shown in the prior art. See MPEP §2143, Ninth Edition, Rev. 07.2022 (Published Feb. 2023).

Claims 1 and 21 recite, inter alia, registering a patient to a pre-operative image to enable the robotic arm to be positionable relative to the anatomical element, reregistering the patient to the pre-operative image based on the notification indicating that the relative pose of the first tracking device and the second tracking device has changed, and automatically positioning a robotic arm relative to an anatomical element after a relative pose of a first tracking device and a second tracking device has changed. None of the cited references taken together or separately appear to disclose, teach, or suggest the features recited in the amended claims.
Nikou teaches a system for performing a computer-aided surgical procedure in which

optical sensors detect and record the location of one or more optical tracking devices mounted to a patient. Nikou, Abstract. The Office Action relies on Nikou as teaching a registration process and registration process and points to "a pre-operative and intraoperative surgical plan is developed. The intraoperative surgical plan is interpreted as registering the patient." Office Action, pg. 8. However, Applicant respectfully disagrees. Nowhere does Nikou teach that the surgical plan includes a registration or reregistration step. Rather, Nikou teaches that the surgical plan includes steps for completing a surgical procedure such as controlling a power of a reamer in accordance with the surgical plan. Further, Nikou specifically describes a registration process and that "registration between the 3D model and the surgical site is performed prior to the surgical procedure." Nikou, at para. [0164]. Thus, Nowhere does Nikou teach a re-registration process in addition to the registration process explicitly taught as being performed prior to the surgical procedure. Further, Nikou also does not teach automatically positioning a robotic arm relative to an anatomical element after a relative pose of a first tracking device and a second
tracking device has changed as recited in claims 1 and 21. Thus, Nikou does not disclose or teach the claimed limitations of claims 1 and 21.
Hale does not cure the deficiencies of Nikou. Hale teaches generating a model of a

portion of a patient based on images received from a stereo camera and comparing the model to a stored model of the portion of the patient to determine if the patent has moved. Hale, para. [0016]. Hale, however, does not teach registering a patient to a pre-operative image to enable the robotic arm to be positionable relative to the anatomical element, reregistering the patient to the pre-operative image based on the notification indicating that the relative pose of the first tracking device and the second tracking device has changed, and automatically positioning a robotic arm relative to an anatomical element after a relative pose of a first tracking device and a second tracking device has changed as recited in claims 1 and 21. Thus, Hale does not disclose or teach the claimed limitations of claims 1 and 21.

Epstein does not cure the deficiencies of Nikou or Hale. Epstein teaches a method for verifying a spatial registration of an anatomical region by tracking a spatial pose of at least one checkpoint defined within the anatomical region and tracking a spatial pose of a probe tip in proximity to the anatomical region at the checkpoint. Epstein, Abstract. Epstein, however, does not teach registering a patient to a pre-operative image to enable the robotic arm to be positionable relative to the anatomical element, reregistering the patient to the pre-operative image based on the notification indicating that the relative pose of the first tracking device and the second tracking device has changed, and automatically positioning a robotic arm relative to an anatomical element after a relative pose of a first tracking device and a second tracking device has changed as recited in claims 1 and 21. Thus, Epstein does not disclose or teach the claimed limitations of claims 1 and 21.
Singh does not cure the deficiencies of Nikou or Hale. Singh teaches systems and

methods for estimating a pose of an anatomy and a pose of a surgical instrument relative to the anatomy by receiving visual and sensory information indicative of pose of the anatomy and surgical instruments relative to the anatomy. Singh, Abstract. Singh, however, does not teach registering a patient to a pre-operative image to enable the robotic arm to be precisely positionable relative to the anatomical element, reregistering the patient to the pre-operative image based on the notification indicating that the relative pose of the first tracking device and the second tracking device has changed, and automatically positioning a robotic arm relative to

an anatomical element after a relative pose of a first tracking device and a second tracking device has changed as recited in claims 1 and 21. Thus, Singh does not disclose or teach the claimed limitations of claims 1 and 21.
Accordingly, the combination of Nikou, Hale, Epstein, and/or Singh fails to disclose
every limitation of claims 1-4, 6-8, and 21-23, and for at least this reason, Applicant respectfully requests that the rejection of claims 1-8 under 35 U.S.C. § 103 be withdrawn.

Based upon the foregoing, Applicant believes that all pending claims are in condition for allowance and such disposition is respectfully requested. Applicant does not acquiesce to any objection, rejection, or argument not specifically addressed herein. Rather, Applicant believes the amendments and arguments contained herein overcome all objections, rejections, or arguments. In the event that a telephone conversation would further prosecution and/or expedite allowance, the Examiner is invited to contact the undersigned.
Respectfully submitted,
SHERIDAN ROSS P.C.
